translationRepairs: Li Kui, whose courtesy name was Duanching, came from Longxi Chenji but his family had long lived in Zhengzhou, where for generations they ranked among the foremost great houses.
Li Kui, whose courtesy name was Duanqing, came from Longxi Chengji but his family had long lived in Zhengzhou, where for generations they ranked among the foremost great houses.
s0001 字端卿 and 隴西成紀 require courtesy-name Duanqing and place Chengji; Duanching and Chenji are romanization errors.
Li Kui, styled Duanching, was a native of Longxi Chenji but his family resided in Zhengzhou; for generations they were a leading clan.
Li Kui, styled Duanqing, was a native of Longxi Chengji but his family resided in Zhengzhou; for generations they were a leading clan.
The literal field repeats the same 端卿→Duanching and 成紀→Chenji errors; Duanqing and Chengji are correct.

He was descended from Xuandao, who had served as a scholar in the Prince of Qin's household and as a superviser-remonstrator, and was the son of Chengyu, Director of the Secretariat, who was posthumously made Minister of Personnel.

He was the great-great-grandson of Xuandao, who had served as a scholar in the Prince of Qin's household and as a supervising remonstrator, and was the son of Chengyu, Director of the Secretariat, who was posthumously made Minister of Personnel.
s0002 玄孫 is the fourth-generation descendant (great-great-grandson), not a vague 'descended from'; 給事中 is supervising remonstrator, and 'superviser' is misspelled.

He was the great-grandson of Xuandao, a scholar of the Prince of Qin's household and a superviser-remonstrator; and the son of Chengyu, Director of the Secretariat and posthumously Minister of Personnel.

He was the great-great-grandson of Xuandao, a scholar of the Prince of Qin's household and a supervising remonstrator; and the son of Chengyu, Director of the Secretariat and posthumously Minister of Personnel.
Literal 'great-grandson' understates 玄孫; great-great-grandson is the correct kinship term, and supervising remonstrator fixes the office spelling.
He was then made Right Supplementation-reminder and Attendant of the Heir Apparent, with responsibility for memorials from members of the imperial clan.
He was then made Right Supplementation-reminder and Imperial Diarist, with responsibility for memorials from members of the imperial clan.
s0005 起居郎 is the Imperial Diarist office, not Attendant of the Heir Apparent.
He was transferred to Right Supplementation-reminder and Attendant of the Heir Apparent, and was charged with imperial-clan memorials.
He was transferred to Right Supplementation-reminder and Imperial Diarist, and was charged with imperial-clan memorials.
The literal likewise misrenders 起居郎 as Attendant of the Heir Apparent; Imperial Diarist matches the Chinese office.
He rose to outer office director in the Ministry of Personnel and bureau director in the Ministry of Rites, serving in both offices as a drafter of imperial rescripts.
He rose to outer office director of the Bureau of Merits and bureau director of Evaluations in the Ministry of Personnel, serving in both offices as a drafter of imperial rescripts.
s0006 司勛員外郎 and 考功郎中 are both Personnel posts (Bureau of Merits; Evaluations); assigning 考功 to the Ministry of Rites is wrong.
He was promoted to outer office director in the Ministry of Personnel and bureau director in the Ministry of Rites, and in both posts drafted imperial rescripts.
He was promoted to outer office director of the Bureau of Merits and bureau director of Evaluations in the Ministry of Personnel, and in both posts drafted imperial rescripts.
Literal repeats the Ministry of Rites error for 考功郎中; both offices belong under the Ministry of Personnel.

His colleague Lü Yin, though far beneath him in birth and standing, had once outranked him in government. After leaving the chief ministership Lü went from imperial guest to military commissioner of Jingnan, where his reputation flourished.

His colleague Lü Yin, though far beneath him in birth and standing, surpassed him in government affairs. After leaving the chief ministership Lü went from imperial guest to military commissioner of Jingnan, where his reputation flourished.

s0034 政事在揆之右 means Lü's governance was superior to Kui's, not that he had outranked him in office; the proposal's sense is right, but 'in handling of government affairs' is awkward, so the phrasing is tightened.

Yin submitted a secret memorial in his own defense, and Kui was demoted to senior administrator of Laizhou. The edict declared, "He stirred up the eight prefectures south of the lake and obstructed control from Jiangling."

Yin submitted a secret memorial in his own defense, and Kui was demoted to senior administrator of Laizhou with concurrent regular status. The edict declared, "He stirred up the eight prefectures south of the lake and obstructed control from Jiangling."
s0036 萊州長史同正員 includes concurrent regular status; idiomatic English wrongly drops 同正員.
Soon someone said: "When Han was formerly Vice Director of the Imperial Clan Court he said nothing; now as Junior Tutor he presumptuously submitted this opinion."
Soon someone said: "When Han was formerly Vice Director of the Imperial Clan Court he said nothing; now as Junior Tutor, his aide presumptuously submitted this opinion."
s0068 妄有奏議, clarified by s0069 呂渭僭陳章奏…為其本使, attributes the presumptuous memorial to Han's aide, not to Han himself; the literal wrongly makes Han the submitter.
